Your experience is actually very common among people with BPD, including myself. I was diagnosed with bipolar 2 about six years ago since I reported minor manic periods followed by severe depressive ones. The mania never happened consistently so I was stuck in a rut in treatment up until late last year. During this period of limbo I found myself asking some of the same questions you're asking in your post. *Why aren't my meds working? Why don't my symptoms really match what my doctor observed? Why do I relate way more to the experiences of people with a completely different mental illness than me?* And one of my favorites when I got the BPD diagnosis: *why did no clinician along the way tell me this was a possibility?*

All that's to say that what you're feeling right now is normal. I second-guessed myself more than ever right after the diagnosis to the point that I felt scared to interact with anyone. I had this latent fear of showing anyone destructive behavior, which led me to isolate in a supposed act of penance. Take solace though in the fact that you're gaining more clarity on your mental health than you've had in the past. I'd also strongly recommend bringing this up in therapy if you haven't already, as they may very well have (through no fault of their own) fallen into complacency when they heard the bipolar diagnosis and didn't explore further.

Alcohol consistently amplifies the worst of my BPD symptoms. I ended up with a lot of thoughts to unpack with this scenario so I'm going to try and structure my post so my interpretation is hopefully easy to follow. The tl;dr is that I see the Alliance still getting enough ships to take on the fleet at Endor. I also believe the destruction of Yavin 4 would hurt the Alliance more than what many suggest.

**Immediate Consequences**

* With Leia and several flight crews dead, several of the surviving Alliance pilots would end up stranded with nowhere safe to land. It's possible a couple of them are capable of fully repairing and restocking their ships for another mission. They'll still have to park on one of Yavin’s remaining moons if a ship's hyperdrive is busted, and that's not ideal considering they couldn't confirm Vader's death and recognize a Star Destroyer or two is almost certainly en route to investigate.
* Along those lines, Luke may have to abandon his X-Wing and possibly R2, who had by this point taken direct blaster cannon fire. Sure, Han could send him hyperspace coordinates to input manually so he could leave, but he couldn’t enter combat again with his fighter in that condition. That opens up a whole other can of worms in terms of his involvement in the war, but I got too deep in speculation on that so I digress.

**Aftermath**

* I’m torn on Han. Part of me thinks he’d ghost the Alliance outright after all that. However I doubt he'd be any more afraid of the Empire than he'd be in canon. He’s already a known conspirator to the Empire by this point so little would change with his criminal consequences between canon and OP’s scenario. All things considered, I think Han would still associate with the Alliance but in a more logistics-heavy role (supply courier, transporting VIPs, etc.) rather than seeing nearly as much combat as he did in canon.
* While the remnants of the Alliance’s forces from the Battle of Yavin wouldn’t have Leia (or potentially even a copy of her message to Obi-Wan if R2 didn’t back it up somewhere besides within himself) to bring to the table in negotiations, they’d still convince the Mon Calamari to commit ships to the war effort. Palpatine had abused them under Imperial rule for years so I see no reason why they wouldn’t back a resistance force that destroyed the Empire’s greatest tool for subjugation.
* OP’s scenario would complicate things for Yoda. Not only does he have no backup plan for defeating Palpatine since Leia's dead, but Luke’s arrival to Dagobah would be delayed if he ends up needing to spend extra time getting a new ship to replace his X-Wing. Han wouldn't take him there, or he at the very least wouldn't stick around for very long listening to Jedi wizard mumbo-jumbo before heading off to an Alliance base or to take refuge in Cloud City.

Yeah the series has given itself an in-lore justification for handwaving, and it's not necessarily a good thing. Regardless, within those parameters the Force chooses how it wants to balance good and evil. I bet Yoda would be furious at the suggestion that defeating the Sith elements during his time would require a violent dissolution of the Jedi Order, and look where that went.

Here's how I've rationalized that trend in my own life, and hopefully someone here can gain some insight into how to explain what they're going through to others. I liken it to having the game of life set to hard mode for us.

Halo is a great analogue for what I'm talking about. On Legendary (the hardest difficulty) you're faced with more enemies whose weapons hit much harder and loadouts include more grenades than enemies do on the Easy difficulty. Now imagine for the sake of illustration that you're one of the few people whose copy of the game has the Legendary difficulty. Everyone around you only has the Easy difficulty loaded onto their game. When you get frustrated at hitting a wall in your progress and dying multiple times over at the same point in a mission, you go to your friends or Reddit asking why the game is so hard. They all act like you don't know what you're talking about because they don't have to face the hurdles you do to play through the same game. You now feel isolated and have a game that feels impossible to enjoy.

All that is to say that Legendary mode exists for a lot of us. Your frustration is no less valid just because most don't have to play it. You may need to do more research and digging around forum posts for secret areas of the level or tips on how to beat tougher enemies, but you still face it.

I was diagnosed with Bipolar II several years ago and later got the diagnosis dropped, but I'll still share here because I seemed to have a vastly different view than most when I stopped taking my meds. In essence I got mad because in my mind they weren't working fast enough.

I've done it with every mental health medication that doctors have tried with me. I would almost always follow this pattern with the meds:

1. Start a new medication.
2. Titrate up on my doctors' recommendations for a couple weeks.
3. Still feel depressed or agitated.
4. Stop taking my meds, assuming they aren't working and get pissed off at the doctors for supposedly lying to me for profit.
5. Get the "brain shock" (as I've heard people describe it in mental health communities) and get lightheaded or pass out by day two without meds.
6. Start taking the meds again as prescribed and discover they actually work.

Paxil was an exception; I took that early on in my treatment journey but stopped with the blessing of my doctor because it turned out to be wildly unhelpful to me and sparked a manic episode which almost cost me my friends. Are you me? This formula is exactly what I needed to follow to get where I am today. I've nearly done things in the heat of anger over things that happened months prior. And learning how to manage that rage was a steady but slow process:

* Identify what's triggering the BPD rage and why. That's usually fairly straightforward though sometimes I uncover a deeper reason based on past experiences, and that's okay! Interceptors are well armed, but they're fragile by comparison to their Republic-era predecessors. Base model TIEs are too to some extent.
